A counter wired to `sceneDidBecomeActive` fires again after every Face ID prompt, Control Center swipe and app-switcher peek, so it is counting interruptions; the transition you want is `sceneWillEnterForeground`.

### Cold launch, in order
1. `application(_:willFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`
2. `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`
3. `application(_:configurationForConnecting:options:)`
4. `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)` — the window is built here
5. `sceneWillEnterForeground(_:)`
6. `sceneDidBecomeActive(_:)`

### Resume from the app switcher
- Only the last two run. The process was alive, so nothing in `didFinishLaunching` fires again — which is why one-time setup put in a scene callback runs twice and one-time setup put in `didFinishLaunching` never re-runs after a resume.
- A brief interruption never reaches the background at all: `sceneWillResignActive` then `sceneDidBecomeActive`, with no foreground pair around it.
- With a scene manifest in `Info.plist`, the AppDelegate's `applicationDidBecomeActive` and `applicationDidEnterBackground` are not called at all — the scene delegate owns those.

The trap on the other side: `didFinishLaunching` also runs when the system launches you into the background for a silent push, a `BGTaskScheduler` task or a finished background download. The user saw nothing, so a session counted there is a phantom. Guard with `UIApplication.shared.applicationState == .background`.

Rule of thumb: a session starts on a foreground entry after an idle gap, not on "active". In SwiftUI the same signal is `scenePhase`, and `.inactive` is the interruption state, so compare against the previous phase rather than reacting to `.active`.

Almost certainly jetsam: the kernel reclaimed your suspended process under memory pressure, and a suspended app gets no callback at all, so anything not written down by `sceneDidEnterBackground` was lost before the user ever came back.

### The three states people confuse
- **Background** — a few seconds of real execution after the user leaves, extended only by `beginBackgroundTask` or an entitled background mode.
- **Suspended** — still in memory, frozen, zero CPU. Coming back is instant and every object is exactly as it was, which is why this case never shows up in testing.
- **Terminated** — the process is gone. The next tap is a full cold launch.

### What the system reclaims, and in what order
- Under memory pressure jetsam kills suspended apps first, worst offenders by footprint and lowest priority band first. The foreground app is last, but it still dies on its own per-process footprint limit.
- Killed while suspended means no `applicationWillTerminate`, no `sceneDidDisconnect`, no warning. `applicationWillTerminate` only runs for an app still executing in the background, so it must never be your only save point.
- A footprint breach is logged as `EXC_RESOURCE`; system-wide pressure produces a JetsamEvent report. MetricKit's `MXAppExitMetric` gives you the split across real users — memory-resource kills versus watchdogs versus the user force-quitting.

The user cannot tell any of this apart, because the switcher still shows the snapshot taken as you resigned active. They tap, get the launch screen, and call it a crash.

Rule of thumb: backgrounding is the last moment you are guaranteed to run. Save there, and restore from disk rather than from memory.

You get seconds, not minutes, and an identifier that is never ended gets the process killed by the watchdog with exception code `0x8badf00d` — which users experience as "the app crashes when I switch away".

### What the call really does
- It asks the system not to suspend you yet. Call it *before* the work starts, while you are still foreground; asking after you are already backgrounded may hand you `.invalid`, which you must check for.
- Apple documents the grant as "a few minutes at most"; on current iOS it is commonly around thirty seconds. Read `UIApplication.shared.backgroundTimeRemaining` instead of assuming a number — it is `greatestFiniteMagnitude` while you are in the foreground.
- Identifiers nest. The app is only suspended once every outstanding one has been ended, so a leaked identifier from an unrelated feature spends your whole budget.

### The expiration handler is not optional
- It runs on the main thread shortly before the budget expires. It must cancel the work and call `endBackgroundTask` synchronously — parking that call in a network completion that may never arrive is exactly the bug that produces the watchdog kill.
- End each identifier exactly once and reset your stored value to `.invalid`; ending the same identifier twice is also a crash.

Use it for genuine task completion — flushing a write, finishing an in-flight request. For anything longer, a background `URLSession` survives suspension and relaunches the app when the transfer finishes, `BGProcessingTask` handles deferrable work, and iOS 26's `BGContinuedProcessingTask` covers user-started work with a system progress UI.

That it is a guaranteed rejection under App Review guideline 2.5.4: a background mode may only be used for the purpose it names, and declaring `audio` without playing audible content the user asked for is the textbook example Apple cites.

### What each key actually buys you
- `audio` — playback, recording, AirPlay and Picture in Picture. The reviewer expects lock-screen controls and a `MPNowPlayingInfoCenter` entry.
- `location` — continuous location updates, with the status-bar indicator the user can see.
- `fetch` and `processing` — the two `BGTaskScheduler` modes: `fetch` for `BGAppRefreshTask`, `processing` for `BGProcessingTask`. Both also need their identifiers listed under `BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers`.
- `remote-notification` — lets a `content-available` push run your code.
- `voip`, `bluetooth-central`, `bluetooth-peripheral`, `external-accessory`, `nearby-interaction`, `push-to-talk` — each tied to a specific framework, and iOS 26 adds a continued-processing mode for `BGContinuedProcessingTask`.

### The evidence a reviewer asks for
- `location`: which feature needs Always, purpose strings that name the user benefit, the battery-life warning in your own UI, and usually a demo video plus a test account.
- `voip`: PushKit paired with CallKit, reporting every VoIP push to CallKit immediately — miss that and iOS stops delivering them at all.
- `bluetooth-*` and `external-accessory`: the actual hardware, described, and MFi for accessories.

Build the sync out of what is actually sanctioned: a `BGProcessingTask` for the work, a background `URLSession` for the transfers, a silent push as a hint, and the same sync repeated on next foreground because none of it is guaranteed. A mode you declare and never exercise is itself a rejection risk.
code_example:
<!-- Info.plist — declare only what the app genuinely does -->
<key>UIBackgroundModes</key>
<array>
  <!-- Required for BGAppRefreshTask (short content refreshes) -->
  <string>fetch</string>
  <!-- Required for BGProcessingTask (longer, charger-friendly work) -->
  <string>processing</string>
  <!-- Required before a content-available push can run your code -->
  <string>remote-notification</string>
  <!-- NOT this: no audible playback in the app -> guideline 2.5.4 rejection
  <string>audio</string>
  -->
</array>

<!-- Every BGTaskScheduler identifier must be listed here as well,
     or submit() throws BGTaskScheduler.Error.Code.notPermitted -->
<key>BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers</key>
<array>
  <string>com.example.app.refresh</string>
  <string>com.example.app.nightly-sync</string>
</array>

<!-- Purpose strings are what the reviewer reads. Name the benefit,
     not the API: "so we can alert you when a delivery is nearby". -->
<key>NSLocationAlwaysAndWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>Alerts you when a delivery reaches your street, even with the app closed.</string>
<key>NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>Shows your position on the delivery map.</string>

answer:
Check the three things that silently disable it before you blame the system: registration that happens after `didFinishLaunching` has returned, an identifier missing from `BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers`, and a handler that never submits the next request.

### Picking the right task first
- `BGAppRefreshTask` — tens of seconds, for pulling fresh content before the user opens the app. Needs the `fetch` background mode.
- `BGProcessingTask` — minutes, with `requiresExternalPower` and `requiresNetworkConnectivity`. This is the nightly sync; the system typically runs it overnight while the device is charging and idle.
- `BGContinuedProcessingTask` (iOS 26) — not a scheduler at all: work the user just started that must finish now, submitted from the foreground and shown with a system progress UI.

### Why it never fires
- `earliestBeginDate` is a floor, never a schedule. The system decides from on-device usage patterns, so an app opened once a month is woken about that often.
- Background App Refresh switched off for the app, Low Power Mode, or the user having force-quit from the switcher: nothing runs at all.
- One pending request per identifier. A resubmit replaces the pending one, and a handler that forgets to resubmit gets exactly one run, ever.
- `submit()` throws — `.notPermitted` for a missing plist entry, `.tooManyPendingTaskRequests` — and `try?` is how teams hide that for a whole release.
- Failing to call `setTaskCompleted(success:)` before the expiration handler fires gets you killed and deprioritised next time.
- The Simulator never runs these tasks; only a device does.

Log `getPendingTaskRequests()` at launch so you can see what the system is actually holding, and always run the same sync on next foreground — the background pass is an optimisation, not the mechanism.

Pause the debugger once the request has been submitted and launch the task by hand from LLDB — `_simulateLaunchForTaskWithIdentifier:` calls your registered launch handler immediately.

### The recipe
1. Run on a real device from Xcode. The Simulator never runs `BGTaskScheduler` tasks.
2. Let the app reach `submit()`, then send it to the background and hit Pause in Xcode.
3. Run the simulate-launch expression against your identifier, then continue. Your handler runs on the spot.
4. For the other half, pause again and call `_simulateExpirationForTaskWithIdentifier:` — same shape, and it fires the `expirationHandler` so you can prove you call `setTaskCompleted(success:)` on that path too.

These are private, undocumented methods that exist for exactly this purpose; they are a debugging aid, never something you ship a call to.

### What it does not simulate
- Whether the system would ever have scheduled you. `earliestBeginDate`, `requiresExternalPower`, the on-device usage model, Low Power Mode and Background App Refresh being off are all bypassed.
- The real time budget. With the debugger attached the watchdog is disabled, so a handler that takes four minutes looks perfectly healthy and dies in the field.
- A cold background launch. The process is already warm and was just foregrounded, so anything in your launch path that quietly assumes a live UI stays untested.
- Throttling — after a force-quit, or after a run you never completed.

So use it to verify the code path, and verify the *scheduling* separately: log `getPendingTaskRequests()` at launch, put an `os_log` line inside the handler, and read Console the next morning to see whether a real run ever happened.

A device token is neither an identity nor permanent — it changes on reinstall, on restore to a new device, when the system invalidates it, and between the sandbox and production APNs environments — so it has to be re-uploaded on every launch, not once.

### The round trip
1. `registerForRemoteNotifications()` on the main thread. Permission for *alerts* is a separate `UNUserNotificationCenter` request; a silent push needs a token but no alert permission.
2. `application(_:didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken:)` hands you 32 bytes of `Data`, asynchronously, possibly after your first screen is already up. Failures arrive in `didFailToRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithError` — log them, they are usually a provisioning or entitlement problem.
3. You hex-encode the bytes and upload them with the user id, bundle id, build environment and locale.

The classic bug is step 3: `deviceToken.description` printed usable hex years ago and now prints `{length = 32, bytes = 0x...}`, so a team ships a token column full of that string and nobody notices until a support ticket.

### What the server must do with it
- Store the environment beside the token. A development-signed build gets a sandbox token that only `api.sandbox.push.apple.com` accepts; TestFlight and App Store builds get production tokens for `api.push.apple.com`. Crossing the two is the `400 BadDeviceToken` every team hits once.
- Treat `410 Unregistered` as a delete rather than a retry — it is the only reliable signal that your app is gone from that device, and the timestamp it carries tells you whether a newer registration already supersedes it.
- Key rows on user *and* token, upserted on every launch: one device hosts several accounts and one account several devices, so a mapping you never clear on logout sends the previous user's notifications to whoever signs in next.

The token identifies an installation, the user id identifies a person, and only the pair is safe to send to.

Start with the headers, not the payload: a background push must be sent with `apns-push-type: background` and `apns-priority: 5`, and APNs rejects priority 10 on a background push with `BadPriority` before it ever reaches the device.

### Getting it delivered at all
- The `aps` dictionary must contain `"content-available": 1` and nothing user-visible. Adding `alert`, `sound` or `badge` turns it into an ordinary notification and you lose the guaranteed background wake — send the two separately.
- `UIBackgroundModes` must include `remote-notification`, and you must implement `application(_:didReceiveRemoteNotification:fetchCompletionHandler:)`.
- Call that completion handler within roughly 30 seconds with an honest `UIBackgroundFetchResult`. Always answering `.noData` teaches the system you are not worth waking.
- Read the APNs response. A 4xx with the `apns-id` in hand proves the push never left your side.

### Delivered, and still ignored
- Low Power Mode, or Background App Refresh turned off for your app: background pushes stop waking it.
- The user force-quit the app from the switcher.
- The system budgets background wakeups per app and coalesces them, so one push per data change is precisely how you get throttled. `apns-expiration: 0` means "drop it if it cannot be delivered right now", and while a device is offline APNs keeps only the most recent notification per token.

The mental model: a silent push is a hint that something changed, never a delivery mechanism. Send one collapsible nudge with `apns-collapse-id`, sync on wake, and sync again on next foreground — because on any given day a meaningful share of your users will never have been woken at all.

The notification service extension is the only place that can rewrite an incoming payload before iOS shows it, so decryption and attachment downloads live there; the content extension only draws custom UI after the user expands a notification whose text is already decided.

### Service extension
- `UNNotificationServiceExtension` runs only for an alert push carrying `"mutable-content": 1`. A silent push never reaches it.
- `didReceive(_:withContentHandler:)` hands you a mutable copy of the content: decrypt into `title` and `body`, add a downloaded file as a `UNNotificationAttachment`, set `threadIdentifier`, or re-issue the content through a communication intent so it renders with the sender's avatar.
- You get roughly 30 seconds of wall clock and a memory ceiling measured in tens of megabytes, not hundreds.
- `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire()` is the last call: hand back the best-attempt content you have been building. If you never call the handler at all, the system delivers the original payload — ciphertext and all.

### Content extension
- `UNNotificationContentExtension` is a view controller bound to a category through `UNNotificationExtensionCategory` in its own Info.plist, and it appears when the notification is expanded.
- It cannot change the payload. Whatever the service extension left is what the banner already said.

### What the budget forces
- Build a best-attempt copy first and mutate it incrementally, so there is always something shippable.
- Download the smallest asset that will do, with your own timeout well under 30 seconds.
- Do nothing that must complete. The process is killed the moment you call the handler, so an analytics flush or a database write started there may simply never happen — hand that work to the app through the shared App Group container instead.

Nothing is shown while the app is frontmost unless `userNotificationCenter(_:willPresent:withCompletionHandler:)` says so, and the buttons come from a `UNNotificationCategory` you register at launch and name in the payload's `category` key.

### Where the buttons come from
- `UNNotificationAction(identifier:title:options:)` builds one button. `.foreground` opens the app; without it your handler runs in the background with seconds to work. `.destructive` colours it red, and `UNTextInputNotificationAction` gives an inline reply field.
- Group them into a `UNNotificationCategory` and register the whole set once with `setNotificationCategories(_:)`. The push then carries `"category": "MESSAGE"` inside `aps`, and the system matches it by identifier.

### The two delegate callbacks
- `willPresent` fires only while the app is in the foreground. Return `[]` to swallow a notification for the chat that is already open, or `[.banner, .list, .sound]` otherwise — `.alert` was split into `.banner` and `.list` in iOS 14.
- `didReceive response:` fires for every tap and every action, foreground or not. `response.actionIdentifier` is `UNNotificationDefaultActionIdentifier` for a tap on the body itself, `UNNotificationDismissActionIdentifier` for a swipe-away (only if the category asked for `.customDismissAction`), and inline text arrives as `UNTextInputNotificationResponse.userText`.

### The trap
Assign the delegate inside `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`, before it returns. When a tap is what launched the app, the system delivers the response immediately after launch; if the delegate is still `nil` at that moment the response is dropped, the app opens on its default screen, and the bug looks like a routing problem rather than a timing one.

`willPresent` decides what is shown; `didReceive` decides what happens. Routing belongs in the second one, never the first.

Adding `.provisional` to the options makes `requestAuthorization` return `true` without ever showing a prompt, in exchange for quiet delivery: the notifications go straight into Notification Center with no banner, no sound and no lock-screen alert.

- The user sees "Keep..." / "Turn Off" buttons on the notification itself. Keeping it promotes you to prominent delivery; turning it off moves you to `.denied`, and from there the only route back is Settings.
- You still get a real device token — `registerForRemoteNotifications()` works under provisional authorisation, so APNs delivery is genuine, just muted.

### The authorisation states
- `.notDetermined` — you may still ask.
- `.provisional` — the quiet trial above.
- `.authorized` — the user said yes explicitly.
- `.denied` — asking again does nothing; send them to `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`.
- `.ephemeral` — App Clips only, and it dies with the clip.

### Authorised does not mean visible
`UNNotificationSettings` carries a separate setting per surface: `alertSetting`, `soundSetting`, `badgeSetting`, `lockScreenSetting`, `notificationCenterSetting`, `timeSensitiveSetting`. A user can be `.authorized` with every banner switched off, sitting inside a Focus, or with Scheduled Summary batching your notification to 6pm. Read those settings before you blame APNs for a "nothing was delivered" report, and pass `.providesAppNotificationSettings` if you want your own settings screen linked from the system one.

The pattern that works: request provisionally at first launch, earn the promotion with the first handful of notifications, and only put up a real prompt at the moment the user has just asked for something that needs one.

Start at the association file: `https://<domain>/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` must return JSON over HTTPS with no redirect, no query string and no authentication, and it must list your `TEAMID.bundle.id` against a path that matches the link.

### What the file and the app must contain
- An `applinks.details` entry with `appIDs` and a `components` array — `{"/": "/items/*"}`, plus optional `?`, `#` and `"exclude": true` rules. The old flat `paths` array still works, but `components` is the current form.
- The Associated Domains capability with `applinks:example.com`, present in the provisioning profile the build was actually signed with. A missing entitlement fails silently and looks exactly like a bad file.

### Why your fix does not show up
Since iOS 14 the device does not fetch your file at all — it asks Apple's CDN, which caches the copy it took for a day or more. Editing the file changes nothing on a phone that already has the old one. `applinks:example.com?mode=developer` makes that device fetch your server directly and needs Developer Mode enabled in Settings.

### The rest of the checklist
- A link to `example.com` tapped on a page already served from `example.com` never opens the app, and neither does a URL typed into the address bar.
- The user may have tapped the domain breadcrumb in Safari's top-right once. That choice sticks per domain until they long-press a link and choose Open in your app again.
- On device: Settings, Developer, Universal Links, Diagnostics. On a Mac: `swcutil dl -d example.com`, with Console filtered to the `swcd` process.
- Handle it in `scene(_:continue:)` and in `connectionOptions.userActivities` for a cold launch — SwiftUI's `.onOpenURL` covers both — and treat the URL as untrusted input, because anyone can type it.

One `NSUserActivity` per scene, holding identifiers rather than objects — that is the only thing the system preserves for a disconnected scene, and everything that was on screen has to be reconstructible from it.

### Where the activity comes from and goes back to
- UIKit: the scene delegate returns one from `stateRestorationActivity(for:)` when the scene disconnects, and reads it back from `session.stateRestorationActivity` in `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)`. The old `restorationIdentifier` and `UIStateRestoring` encoding path is deprecated and does not run for scene-based apps at all.
- SwiftUI: `.userActivity(_:isActive:_:)` fills the activity and `.onContinueUserActivity(_:)` restores it, while `@SceneStorage` covers the small per-window details — selected tab, scroll target, an unsent draft.

### Rules the payload has to obey
- `userInfo` takes property-list types and a few kilobytes at most. Store `postID`, never the post.
- Every screen must be reachable from an id alone. A screen you can only get to by having pushed the previous one is a screen neither restoration nor a deep link can rebuild.
- `stateRestorationActivity(for:)` is called at disconnect time, not continuously, so keep the truth in a model you can serialise on demand rather than scattered across view controllers.

### What throws the state away
Force-quitting discards the saved state for every window, and iOS drops it rather than restoring you into a launch that just crashed. So restoration is a nicety, never the only copy of something the user typed — real drafts belong in your own storage. The same activity object is what `requestSceneSessionActivation(_:userActivity:options:errorHandler:)` uses to open a fourth window, which is the cheap way to test all of this.

The system is prewarming your app: since iOS 15 it starts the process ahead of a predicted launch, runs dyld, the Objective-C runtime and your static initialisers, then stops just short of `UIApplicationMain` and leaves the process sitting there — so process start time can be minutes before the tap.

### What runs and what does not
- dyld linking, `+load` methods, C++ static constructors and any global whose initialiser does real work — all of that happens at prewarm time, on the system's schedule, with the phone in a pocket.
- `main` is entered but `UIApplicationMain` is never called, so `didFinishLaunching`, scene connection and your first frame all still wait for the real launch.
- Therefore anything anchored at process start — `kinfo_proc.p_starttime`, or a `let start = CFAbsoluteTimeGetCurrent()` in a file-scope global — measures the system's whim, not the user's wait.

### What to measure instead
- Detect it: `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["ActivePrewarm"] == "1"` on a prewarmed launch. Bucket those samples separately or drop them; never average them in.
- Anchor your own signposts at `didFinishLaunching` (or `willEnterForeground` for a warm resume) and close them on the first real frame, from a `CATransaction` completion after the root view is on screen.
- In the field, `MXAppLaunchMetric` gives you `histogrammedOptimizedTimeToFirstDraw` next to `histogrammedTimeToFirstDraw`; the optimised histogram accounts for prewarming and is the one to trend.

Prewarming is free speed only while your static-initialisation phase is cheap and free of side effects. A singleton that opens a database, stamps a session id or fires a network call from its initialiser now does all of that at a random moment, possibly minutes before the user exists.

The system relaunched it straight into the background — a silent push, a `BGTaskScheduler` task, a finished background `URLSession`, a location or Bluetooth event — and the very same `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` runs, only with `applicationState == .background` and, usually, no scene ever connected.

### How to tell
- `UIApplication.shared.applicationState == .background` inside `didFinishLaunching` is the check. `launchOptions` also names the reason: `.remoteNotification`, `.location`, `.bluetoothCentrals`, `.url`.
- Under the SwiftUI lifecycle, `scenePhase` is `.background` and `UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor` still receives the same callback.

### What that path must not do
- Build UI. There is no window to present into, and reaching into view code here is exactly how you get a crash report with no user in sight.
- Read protected data before first unlock. `NSFileProtectionComplete` files are unreadable and `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked` Keychain items fail with `errSecInteractionNotAllowed` — guard on `isProtectedDataAvailable` and wait for `protectedDataDidBecomeAvailableNotification`.
- Bootstrap the whole app. Every SDK, cache warm and migration you run here spends the user's battery on work nobody is looking at, and the budget is seconds.
- Count a session. Analytics that increments "app opens" in `didFinishLaunching` will invent launches that never happened.

### What it must do
Finish fast and call the completion handler — a silent push gives you about 30 seconds, and failing to call back gets your future wake-ups throttled. Keep the work idempotent and cancellable: the same launch may repeat five minutes later, and the process can be suspended mid-flight. The mental model is that a background launch is a short job that happens to share your app's `main`, not a launch of your app.

A swipe in the app switcher marks the app as user-terminated, and from then until the user opens it again or the device reboots, iOS refuses to relaunch it for almost every background trigger.

### Dead until the user comes back
- Silent pushes with `content-available: 1`. Apple is explicit that background notifications are not delivered to an app the user force-quit.
- `BGAppRefreshTask` and `BGProcessingTask`. Submitted `BGTaskRequest`s stay on file, but nothing launches you to run them.
- Background `URLSession` completions and Core Bluetooth state restoration: the events wait rather than waking you.

### Still gets through
- Alert pushes. The banner is drawn by the system, not by your app, so it appears as usual and tapping it launches you normally — as do local `UNNotificationRequest`s that were already scheduled.
- Significant-location change, region monitoring and visit monitoring. These are the documented exception and will relaunch the app even across a reboot.
- PushKit VoIP pushes, which is precisely why calls use them. The price is that since iOS 13 you must report a CallKit call on every one, or the app is killed and eventually cut off from VoIP pushes altogether.

### Why this bites teams
Testers force-quit between runs out of habit and then report that background sync never fires. Reproduce from a *system*-terminated state instead: leave the app suspended and let memory pressure or a reboot take it, because that state still receives everything above. And never let a feature's freshness rest on silent push alone — one swipe turns it off for that user until they return, so the app must also reconcile on foreground.
